text: METR : These conclusions are based on key empirical findings from the full report. Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted. ​ Ajeya Cotra (METR): For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed. Peter Wildeford : It seems important to realize that: - AI companies have unreleased internal models that are more powerful than the public ones we plebs have access to - Only when you account for these internal models, you can see that AI progress is actually accelerating faster than before - AI companies use their AIs with like 10,000x more compute than us plebs, so they can do much more than we can even with the same AIs Benjamin Todd : Extrapolating Anthropic’s internal AI R&D data results in Claude leading internal research by mid-2027, and plausibly near full automation by the end of 2027, lining up with other methods. (h/t @luc_feron ) METR : Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff. METR : In our first section, we share our subjective conclusions about risk . We now believe that: As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025. The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks. Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year. We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute. Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon. We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment. A detailed description of the data we had access to was redacted. A summarized version is as follows: Internal benchmark scores and AECI for internal models, plus sample tasks, rubric answers and agent expenditure on those tasks. Historical data on algorithmic efficiency and overall model strength in pretraining and RL, as well as improvements to compute utilization, inference efficiency and data efficiency. Headcount and attribution of progress to specific staff. Training compute metrics in many relevant domains. Internal analysis on relevant open questions. Internal surveys of self-reported AI uplift by team. Lines of code and pull requests across the company and some research teams. AI agent inference spend over time. Internal documents on autonomous research contributions. ~15 interviews with key staff, covering a predefined but wide scope that excluded particularly sensitive topics. In a small number of cases, Anthropic did not provide relevant information when they deemed it too sensitive.​ Anthropic also offered extensive staff time and expertise to this project. We believe the two staff we worked most closely with are the two highest-context researchers on AI R&D acceleration measurement at Anthropic. Both of these staff met with us frequently for live discussion, and spent substantial time collecting data, doing analysis, and providing feedback. METR : We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative. As a consequence, the public must rely on our judgment more than we consider ideal. METR : While we were able to freely share our highest-level conclusions about risk, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.” Some of these redactions are themselves challenging to describe clearly without revealing sensitive information we have been asked to redact. We share a table of important evidence we were and were not able to discuss given the redactions in our process section below. All redactions that were important for our conclusions are covered by our descriptions in that table or other in-line descriptions in the report below. Much of the redacted evidence we viewed had multiple plausible interpretations, and both METR and Anthropic researchers have significant uncertainty about how to synthesize the evidence into a holistic picture. This makes it hard for the public to judge this evidence themselves, reconcile it with evidence from other sources, and come to their own conclusions (i.e. this report does not achieve ‘transparency about evidence’ ). As a consequence, the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here. METR : Anthropic’s redactions also meant that we could not communicate: Our more detailed estimates of acceleration and attribution to AI usage for key areas of the model training pipeline. Our more detailed breakdown of progress attributable to compute, data and algorithmic progress, other than the key takeaway that “We are confident that the acceleration was not due to acceleration in training compute.” More detailed answers to the limitations questions in our proposal, which would require more discussion of methodological details. Forecasts of metrics for future models. They also made some other more minor redactions throughout, which we attempt to describe in each section of this report. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.” METR : The acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors. We investigated a variety of factors which could have contributed to the observed acceleration in late 2025, but details of many of these factors have been redacted. We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI. This judgment is given with substantial uncertainty, but is based on a variety of lines of evidence on contributions from AI and other causes. We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time, and do not think the other factors we investigated would explain the sustained acceleration. The evidence of speedup from the usage of AI we describe below also seems compatible with a large contribution.​ This includes the following models (these are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames): Unreleased 2022, which finished training in 2022 Model 2, which finished training in July 2026 Model 3, which finished training in August–September 2026 Model 4, which finished training in September–October 2026 METR’s Full Report includes a forecast for a future model, but this was redacted. METR : We use the date at which the model could be used by most Anthropic employees instead of public release dates; this allows us to make apples-to-apples comparisons with unreleased models. These in general show slightly higher degrees of acceleration as Anthropic is holding onto more recent models for slightly longer before their public release. Charles Foster (METR): It’s easy to mistake linear gains in ECI for linear gains in model performance. Each additional point actually *multiplies* a model’s odds of success on every benchmark. For example, historically each 5-point increase in ECI corresponded to roughly a doubling in time horizon. METR : These investigations included attempts to understand: Different methodological variants of internal metrics. We spent multiple weeks on these investigations, and this is our greatest source of uncertainty. The beliefs of staff on the relevant teams about key internal evidence and estimates of acceleration. Whether other parts of the model training pipeline could be biasing our estimates of acceleration, and where adjustments could be applied. Whether Anthropic could be overfitting to internal metrics. We go into detail on potential problems with AECI such as: Anthropic’s internal benchmarks are increasingly saturated: Model 4 achieves greater than 50% on all the AECI benchmarks on which it was tested. However, measured acceleration appears reasonably robust to saturation concerns. Token spend may be too low to maximally elicit models. The logistic link function could be misspecified on a few benchmarks. However, on the whole we think it is a reasonable approximation. There are various reasons why an acceleration in benchmark scores could overstate or understate an acceleration in real-world impacts. AECI assumes that a model’s score on a benchmark is a function of the model’s latent strength, and specifically that the function is logistic (shown below in black). This can be interpreted as an assumption on the distribution of difficulty of tasks in a benchmark, including how many tasks are broken or what fraction can be guessed. The following figure illustrates a few different link functions. The logistic function assumes a symmetric distribution with exponentially declining tails. The log-log function assumes a long tail of hard tasks; the complementary log-log function assumes a long tail of easy tasks. Toby Ord : I don’t think 2x is the best interpretation of this data. It assumes zero level shift from the new Mythos pre-train. If you allow for a level shift from that as well as a slope change, the slope change drops to about 1.4x. METR has released a very interesting report suggesting a recent acceleration in AI capabilities this year at Anthropic due to RSI. But they can’t confidently reject an alternative explanation: the step change you get with the larger pre-train of Mythos. See [ here ]. METR : We define AI speedup as the ratio between a staff member or team’s output with AI and without AI, noting that output can often be difficult to measure or define. We now briefly survey the overall evidence for AI speedup, concluding: There is some evidence for high speedup, though the precise amount of speedup is highly uncertain. Fully autonomous contributions to AI R&D are not currently a large contributor to overall progress, but they may be in the near future. … We have many lines of evidence relevant to AI’s contribution to progress in different parts of the model training pipeline, including interviews, self-reported uplift, headcount, lines of code, experiment usage, and qualitative reflections from leadership. We highlight three important unredacted sources. Both METR and Anthropic interviewed many researchers in detail about the degree of overall acceleration in their area of work attributable to AI use (see details in the appendix below). Our overall impression was a quite wide range of estimates, but centered around a 2x acceleration. Anthropic also shared data on self-reported uplift due to AI from a variety of sources. The most recent data is from a series of Slack polls. … The responses reflect low-effort consideration. Nevertheless, we observe consistent growth in these self-reports, and very high levels (reaching 12x in October 2026), as shown in the chart below. Researchers described significant “signs of life” implying [highly significant and fully autonomous] contributions could occur soon. Ajeya Cotra (METR): Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that. Ajeya Cotra (METR): researcher labor is only one input to discovering these compute multipliers … If we assume a very simple Cobb-Douglas model where experiment compute and labor are similarly important, that means the uplift to labor roughly needs to be the square of the acceleration in compute multipliers. … This would imply that we would need a (~2-3x)^2 = ~4-9x speed up in labor to make overall AI capabilities go twice as fast. Both METR and Anthropic interviewed many researchers (see details in the following section ). We used Claude to classify the quotes according to whether they support 2x or more acceleration from AI in their area of work, relative to working without AI. We interpret the results as mildly in favor of 2x or greater acceleration: Yes: 2 Leans yes: 3 Borderline/unclear: 4 Leans no: 0 No: 2 The quotes, with sensitive details redacted, are in the following section . (E.g., conclusions about whether this speed up is from RSI depend on trust.) I do trust the authors of the report a lot to be careful and rigorous and generally do a good job. (Note that I also work at METR.) Less extensive redactions would greatly reduce this need for trust. Since in my current role I may have access to other confidential information that could be relevant to timelines one way or another, I unfortunately cannot state my all-things-considered views on ASI timelines or the probability of a software intelligence explosion right now . Here, I’ve done some analysis of the implications using my previous public statements. A 2x acceleration in overall AI progress from RSI corresponds to a much larger than 2x RSI speed up for AI software R&D (algorithms and data); I did an estimate using my public preexisting modeling of drivers of AI progress and the public report which yielded a very rough estimate of 4.5x for how much RSI is currently accelerating AI software progress (relative to no AI automation). In the AI 2027 scenario, this much acceleration happens around March 2027. Here are the worked details of this estimate based on my public modeling. There are two main reasons RSI speed up of AI software R&D must be larger: - Not all of AI progress is from better software (some is from scaling up compute in training runs). I’ve previously speculated that around 2/3 of AI progress is from software improvements which implies that 2x overall AI progress acceleration requires 3x faster software progress. - Diminishing returns: A fixed amount of progress requires more work over time, so to ongoingly maintain 3x faster software progress via AI automation, you need increasingly large speed boosts from AI automation (as in, speed ups relative to how fast software R&D would go without AI automation). Based on this report, it seems that there is a substantial amount of additional AI progress from automation that has occurred. We can estimate the effects of diminishing returns by first determining how many additional years of software progress we’ve seen (relative to the preexisting trend) and then estimating how much software R&D would slow down after a year of software progress if you held inputs fixed due to diminishing returns. I’ve previously estimated software R&D would slow down by around 2x for each year of software progress if you held inputs fixed and based on the report, it seems as though we’ve perhaps seen roughly 0.35-1.0 years of additional software progress incorporated into trained models so far (geometric mean of ~0.6). Sam McCandlish (Cofounder, Anthropic): I’m Sam, one of Anthropic’s co-founders, and I lead much of our safety work. I’m going to have more to share on that work over the coming months. I thought I’d start by sharing a few thoughts on the latest report from @METR_Evals . The speed of progress in model capabilities is one of the most important questions in AI safety, and METR’s work here provides the public with an independent, external view into how this is happening inside Anthropic. I’ll talk more about some of the details below, but first some context for those new to this work. How quickly AI progress is accelerating has many important safety implications, since it determines how quickly the risks from advanced models increase. But, because most research happens within the frontier labs, it’s difficult for external observers and policy makers to get a strong sense of what that rate is. We kicked off the process with METR that led to this report earlier in the year, in anticipation of progress continuing to accelerate. For this report, we gave METR access to a range of sensitive internal data, including benchmark scores for unreleased models, estimates of how models are progressing, and interviews with our researchers. They had complete independence to form their own conclusions. Many of their conclusions match my own. AI is speeding up our research, but it’s hard to say exactly how much. While they conclude AI can’t yet make the most important contributions to model training on its own, they think the pace of development could, by default, accelerate further. This work began well before and is separate from the embedded third-party evaluators that are part of our commitment to pacing the frontier, but it’s a good illustration of why we think evaluators are a good idea. The more access reviewers have, the clearer a picture they can form of the situation and the better-positioned they are to highlight situations like this one. We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work. But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster. That would make the risks METR is worried about worse. That’s a tradeoff. I think we made the right call, though we’re continuing to assess the pros and cons here. In the coming weeks, we plan to share a report with our own analysis of the speed of AI progress within Anthropic, including where we stand against our Responsible Scaling Policy, plus new steps we’re taking to strengthen our safety and security practices as AI keeps improving quickly.
